text: The well planning checklist is conclusive proof, but there is also multiple testimonies cited in the briefs saying that they were going to miss the deadline anyway without regard to what was going on in the Dorothy White world. To support its interpretation of this clause, Matador has to convince this court that this is the strangest, broadest, most lessee-friendly force majeure clause that the world deserves. The problem is it just isn't. It's a fairly standard force majeure clause. The clause requires a delay in the leasehold operations. Mr. Gunn conceded that. The clause says when lessee's operations are delayed, but Matador agrees. That means operations on the leasehold estate. But that's a huge problem for Matador in this case, because the events that they talk about weren't on the leasehold estate, and it takes a whole lot of steps and a whole lot of time in order for them to get there. The issue of causation, the language delayed by in the clause, lessee's operations are delayed by an event of force majeure, creates the causation requirement. Now what Matador says is that that creates a very light burden, implies that that's very unusual language. In cases interpreting a clause that says performance is prevented, those aren't useful, because what our clause says is delayed. Well, language like delayed, hinder, or interrupt is an extremely common way in force majeure clauses to talk about the timely performance due that's prevented by force majeure. For example, Gilbert versus Smedley, Gulf Oil versus Southland in this court, those clauses say delayed or interrupted. Sudden Partnership versus Holt, delayed or interrupted. Pearlman versus Pioneer, prevented or hindered. Dorman versus Pan America in the Fifth Circuit, delayed or interrupted. Exploration versus Birdwell, delayed or interrupted. It's an incredibly common way to refer to the performance that is prevented by force majeure in a force majeure clause and in this situation, delayed means made late, and if it doesn't mean made late, the clause doesn't make sense. The whole purpose of force majeure is you have an event that impacts your ability to perform under a contract and therefore if it's out of your control, you're excused from the event. That's the most basic meaning of force majeure, according to Hunter Carvin. And what Sun Oil says, and what a number of other courts, including this court, say is that to the extent that's unclear in this lease that it's about relieving them from obligations because they missed those obligations due to an event of force majeure, then the common law can be used to fill those gaps, to the extent that there are any. Now, Matador makes the argument that you can take causation completely out of force majeure and that you don't have to prove that your contractual obligation was impacted by a force majeure event and they cite the Kleberg case for that. Now, the Kleberg case, first of all, was reversed by the Texas Supreme Court, and secondly, please read that case very carefully. It does not say what appellants say it says. In fact, far from taking causation out of the inquiry, it says that URI did show that the asserted events prevented URI from performing groundwater restoration, which is what the contract required. They're taking URI out because it doesn't say what they claim. There is literally not one single case anywhere where performance is excused under a force majeure clause when that performance wasn't prevented or impacted by the event of force majeure. They are asking this court to create an all new animal by removing causation, even though that delayed by language creates a causation requirement. Next, the event must be non-economic. That's a highly restrictive aspect of this clause that's largely glossed over by appellants that eliminates a lot of potential activities that would otherwise qualify for force majeure. The force majeure needs to be beyond the lessee's control. That's a very common provision. It's more stringent than, say, the hydrocarbon versus tracker clause, which says reasonable control. Oftentimes in a force majeure provision, you have a list of events that are included and then a catch all at the end that says or whatsoever else beyond the reasonable control of the lessee or whatever else beyond the reasonable control of the operator. This clause is actually more restrictive than the most common kind of clause, which includes both a laundry list and a catch all because it doesn't include the laundry list. In this case, Matador is arguing that the wellbore instability qualifies under the catch all and under the tech almost case. That means that they need to establish that it was unforeseeable, a burden that I'll discuss later that they can't. The non-economic and beyond control limit to what can construe force majeure. So the fact that the force majeure needs to be non-economic and beyond the control of the operator is a limitation, but it's not a definition, as we explained in our brief. Now the clause in this case, as your honors pointed out in your questions, needed to be invoked before the lease terminated. What counsel said is we had 60 days to provide notice.
